q: How many types of NRFO operations does the FOM define, and what are they?
a: Three: (1) Flights that must be operated under Part 121, (2) Flights that may be operated under Part 91, and (3) Flights operated under Part 121 Cargo Only.

src.quote: There are three types of NRFO operations
src.note: NRFOs are all flight operations that are not on the published schedule. The type determines the governing rules and Flight Attendant requirements.

q: What three conditions must be met to operate an NRFO under Part 121?
a: The aircraft is on the Operations Specifications, the aircraft is equipped and maintained per the Alaska Airlines Maintenance Program, and the crew is fully qualified.

src.quote: Aircraft is on the Operations Specifications
src.note: All three conditions must be satisfied before a Part 121 NRFO may be dispatched.

q: Are Flight Attendants required on a cargo-only NRFO?
a: No. Flight Attendants are not required on a cargo-only NRFO.

src.quote: Flight Attendants are not required on a cargo-only NRFO.
src.note: Non-essential passengers are also not allowed on flights dispatched as Part 121 – Cargo Only.

q: On a Part 91 NRFO, at what passenger count is a Flight Attendant required to be on board?
a: A Flight Attendant must be on board if more than nineteen (19) passengers are carried.

src.quote: a Flight Attendant must be on board if more than nineteen (19) passengers are carried
src.note: Alaska policy is to use a full complement of Flight Attendants anytime one Flight Attendant is required (14 CFR 91.533).

q: Who may be carried as passengers on a Part 91 flight operated without Flight Attendants?
a: Passengers are restricted to Alaska Air Group employees, unless authorization for non-employees is received from the Director of Operations, FODO, or NRFO Management.

src.quote: Passengers on Part 91 flights without Flight Attendants will be restricted to Alaska Air Group employees
src.note: Non-employees require authorization from the DO, FODO, or NRFO Management.

q: On a Part 91 non-revenue operation, how many Flight Attendants are required for more than 19 but less than 51 passengers?
a: One (1) Flight Attendant.

src.quote: more than 19 but less than 51 passengers – 1
src.note: The full scale: 19 or less – 0; 19 to under 51 – 1; more than 50 but less than 101 – 2; more than 100 – 2 (+1 for each unit of 50).

q: On a Part 91 non-revenue operation, how many Flight Attendants are required with more than 100 passengers on board?
a: Two (2), plus one additional for each unit of 50 passengers.

src.quote: more than 100 passengers on board – 2 (+1 each unit of 50 passengers)
src.note: This scaling applies to positioning and non-revenue misc operations on all-passenger aircraft.

q: Besides crewmembers, name persons who may be carried on a Part 121 NRFO flight without Flight Attendants when approved.
a: Essential Company employees, an FAA Air Carrier Inspector performing official duties, an NTSB official performing official duties, and persons handling or essential to cargo on NRFO cargo-only flights.

src.quote: FAA Air Carrier Inspector performing official duties
src.note: Requires approval by the Director of Operations or NRFO Management designee (14 CFR 121.583). Any other passenger triggers the full FA complement.

q: What is a Positioning Flight?
a: A flight conducted with an airworthy aircraft flown from one destination to another under 14 CFR Part 91 with no revenue passengers or cargo; it can be for maintenance, charter, scheduling, etc.

src.quote: operated under 14 CFR Part 91 with no revenue passengers or cargo
src.note: A positioning flight delivers the empty aircraft to where a charter begins or back into scheduled service after the charter is over.

q: Which Ops Spec authorizes the Special Flight Permit Ferry, and what does it provide?
a: Maintenance Ops Spec D084 is the Special Flight Permit with Continuous Authorization to Conduct Ferry Flights.

src.quote: Maintenance Ops Spec D084 is the Special Flight Permit with Continuous Authorization to Conduct Ferry Flights
src.note: Section references 14 CFR 21.197 and GPM 05-00-05. The permit authorizes flying an aircraft that may not meet applicable airworthiness requirements.

q: May passengers or cargo be carried on a Special Flight Permit Ferry?
a: No. The flight shall not have passengers or cargo.

src.quote: The flight shall not have passengers or cargo.
src.note: If issued without limitations, the flight is limited to Flight Crew, Flight Attendants, and Maintenance Crew.

q: Can MELs be applied to a flight on a Special Flight Permit, and is ETOPS PDC/PDSC required?
a: Yes, MELs may be applied to flights on a Special Flight Permit. ETOPS PDC/PDSC is not required, but aircraft fluid levels will be inspected and serviced as required.

src.quote: MELs may be applied to flights on a Special Flight Permit.
src.note: Certain MEL Remarks/Exceptions and Operations Procedures may not apply, except for ER operations/ETOPS and flight level restrictions.

q: Does a 787 require a Maintenance Check Flight after a double-engine change, and which group is it?
a: Yes. A 787 flight after a double-engine change is a Group 2 Maintenance Check Flight, which must be flown by a qualified Functional Check Pilot.

src.ref: FOM 16.3.2.2 — Classification of Maintenance Check Flights
src.quote: flight after a double-engine change
src.note: Group 2 checks major systems or components to determine airworthiness and may require emergency, abnormal, or special procedures in flight.

q: What are Group 1 and Group 2 Maintenance Check Flights also called?
a: A Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight is also referred to as an 'evaluation flight'; a Group 2 Maintenance Check Flight is also referred to as a 'test flight'.

src.ref: FOM 16.3.2.2 — Classification of Maintenance Check Flights
src.quote: also referred to as an “evaluation flight”
src.note: Group 1 uses normal FCOM procedures; Group 2 involves specialized training and may use emergency, abnormal, or special procedures.

q: Who may crew a Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight, and who is prohibited?
a: It may be flown by a line Captain and a First Officer. A 'High-Minimums Captain' or 'Restricted First Officer' is prohibited from flying a Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight.

src.ref: FOM 16.3.2.2 — Classification of Maintenance Check Flights
src.quote: A “High-Minimums Captain” or “Restricted First Officer” is prohibited from flying a Group 1 Maintenance Check Flight.
src.note: A Group 1 flight is not considered a 'test flight'; the crew is not trained or qualified as test pilots. Group 2 must be flown by a qualified Functional Check Pilot.

q: What two DD Forms is Alaska Airlines issued for use of military airfields, and by whom?
a: DD Form 2401 (Civil Aircraft Landing Permit) and DD Form 2400 (Civil Aircraft Certificate of Insurance), issued by the US Air Force, the US Army, and the US Navy/Marine Corps.

src.ref: FOM 16.1.12 - Military Civil Aircraft Landing Permits and Certificate of Insurance
src.quote: Alaska Airlines is issued DD Form 2401, Civil Aircraft Landing Permit, and DD Form 2400, Civil Aircraft Certificate of Insurance by the US Air Force, the US Army, and the US Navy/Marine Corps.
src.note: A second AF DD Form 2401 authorizes use of all US Air Force Aviation Facilities worldwide for government charters and contract flights (including AMC).

q: Rev 125 change: where does the FOM now list the specific military bases Alaska Airlines may use?
a: It does not. Rev 125 deleted the per-service base lists (former 16.1.12.1, .2 and .3), including the Bucholz AAF exception. Use of US military installations is limited to those specifically authorized in the approved DD Form 2401.

src.ref: FOM 16.1.12 - Military Civil Aircraft Landing Permits and Certificate of Insurance
src.quote: Alaska Airlines is issued DD Form 2401, Civil Aircraft Landing Permit, and DD Form 2400, Civil Aircraft Certificate of Insurance by the US Air Force, the US Army, and the US Navy/Marine Corps.
src.note: The Captain is responsible for knowledge of the limitations in the DD forms; they are located on the EFB in Comply365.

q: How many Maintenance Logbook entries are required for a Special Flight Permit, and what does each describe?
a: Two: the first entry's Defect Description describes the mechanical defect and is resolved as a deferral referencing the Special Flight Permit to move the aircraft; the second entry states an inspection is required and resolves that the aircraft is safe for the intended flight and the Flight Crew has been briefed.

src.quote: two Maintenance Logbook entries are required for a Special Flight Permit
src.note: The Maintenance Logbook with the 'aircraft released' statement and a copy of the ferry authorization, plus Ops Spec D084, must be carried on board.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Maintenance has just completed a double-engine change on a 787 and requests a check flight. What group is this Maintenance Check Flight, who must be at the controls, and under what Part does it operate?
a: It is a Group 2 Maintenance Check Flight (a 'test flight'). It must be flown by a qualified Functional Check Pilot. Like all Maintenance Check Flights, it operates under 14 CFR Part 91, flown for the express purpose of verifying airworthiness.

src.ref: FOM 16.3.2.2 — Classification of Maintenance Check Flights
src.quote: Group 2 Maintenance Check Flights must be flown by a qualified Functional Check Pilot.
src.note: A 787 flight after a double-engine change is a listed Group 2 example. Group 2 involves specialized training and may require emergency, abnormal, or special procedures in flight. Final group categorization is approved by the Director of Operations or the Standards/Part 119 Chief Pilot (16.3.2.1).

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A 787 has a mechanical defect that is being deferred, and it must be flown empty to a maintenance base on a Special Flight Permit Ferry under Ops Spec D084. Can you carry passengers or cargo, may MELs be applied, and how many Maintenance Logbook entries are required?
a: No passengers or cargo may be carried. MELs may be applied to flights on a Special Flight Permit. Two Maintenance Logbook entries are required — one deferring the defect by referencing the Special Flight Permit, and one stating the aircraft is safe for the intended flight and the Flight Crew has been briefed. The Flight Crew shall not perform any troubleshooting or non-standard activities.

src.quote: The flight shall not have passengers or cargo.
src.note: Ops Spec D084 authorizes flying an aircraft that may not meet applicable airworthiness requirements (14 CFR 21.197). ETOPS PDC/PDSC is not required, but aircraft fluid levels are inspected and serviced. Two Maintenance Logbook entries are required per 16.4.2.1.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are positioning a 787 under Part 91 with no Flight Attendants on board, and a non-employee observer asks to ride along. Is that allowed, and whose authorization would it take?
a: By default, no. Passengers on Part 91 flights without Flight Attendants are restricted to Alaska Air Group employees. Carrying a non-employee requires authorization from the Director of Operations, FODO, or NRFO Management.

src.quote: Passengers on Part 91 flights without Flight Attendants will be restricted to Alaska Air Group employees
src.note: Authorization for non-employees comes from the DO, FODO, or NRFO Management (14 CFR 91.533). If a Flight Attendant is required, Alaska policy is to use a full complement.
